title: Panuveitis: The Global Diagnostic Challenge
summary: A textbook-level deep dive into panuveitis, characterized by simultaneous inflammation of the anterior chamber, vitreous, and retina or choroid. This infographic covers the critical etiology, diagnostic workup, and evidence-based management of this sight-threatening condition.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Panuveitis refers to an intraocular inflammation involving the anterior chamber, vitreous, and the posterior segment (retina, choroid, or both). According to the SUN (Standardization of Uveitis Nomenclature) criteria, there must be active inflammation in all three compartments. It accounts for approximately 7-15% of all uveitis cases in tertiary referral centers and carries a high risk of permanent visual impairment if not managed aggressively.

sections.title: Anterior Segment Findings
content: Cells and Flare in the Anterior Chamber (AC)
Keratic Precipitates (KP): Mutton-fat (granulomatous) vs. Fine (non-granulomatous)
Iris Nodules: Koeppe (pupillary border) or Busacca (iris stroma)
Posterior Synechiae: Adhesion of iris to lens
Peripheral Anterior Synechiae (PAS)
Secondary Glaucoma due to trabeculitis or pupil block

sections.title: Posterior Segment Findings
content: Vitreous Cells and Snowballs/Snowbanking (if pars plana involved)
Chorioretinal Lesions (Granulomas in Sarcoid/TB, Dalen-Fuchs in SO/VKH)
Retinal Vasculitis (Sheathing, Exudates, 'Candle-wax drippings' in Sarcoid)
Optic Disc Edema or Hyperemia
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) - most common cause of vision loss
Exudative Retinal Detachment (Common in VKH)

rows: Salt & Pepper Fundus, Acute Syphilitic Posterior Placoid
History of trauma or surgery in the fellow eye

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Thorough history (travel, trauma, systemic symptoms, sexual history).
Step 2: Baseline labs: CBC, ESR, CRP, RPR/FTA-ABS (Syphilis rule-out is mandatory).
Step 3: Rule out TB/Sarcoid: Quantiferon-Gold, Chest X-ray or High-Resolution CT (HRCT).
Step 4: Ocular Imaging: OCT Macula (CME), FFA (Vasculitis/Ischemia), ICG (Choroidal involvement).
Step 5: Ancillary Tests: B-scan (if media opaque), HLA-B51 (Behcet), HLA-DR4 (VKH).
Step 6: Invasive Tests: Aqueous tap or Vitreous biopsy (if masquerade or treatment-resistant infectious suspicion).

sections.title: Emergency Red Flags
content: Rapid, painful vision loss (Suggests ARN or Endophthalmitis)
Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD)
Ischemic Retinal Vasculitis (high risk of NVE/VH)
Sudden 'Sea-fan' Neovascularization
Suspicion of Masquerade (CNS symptoms in elderly + panuveitis)

content.explanation: P: Prodromal (Flu-like, Meningism); A: Acute Uveitic (Exudative RD, thick choroid); C: Convalescent (Sunset-glow fundus, Sugiura sign); R: Recurrent (Chronic AC inflammation).

sections.title: Management Step-Ladder
content: Phase 1: Induction. Oral Prednisone (1mg/kg/day) or IV Methylprednisolone pulses for severe cases.
Phase 2: Local Control. Topical Steroids (Pred Forte q1h) and Cycloplegics (Atropine/Cyclopentolate).
Phase 3: Steroid Sparing. If tapered below 10mg/day fails, start IMT (Methotrexate, Mycophenolate Mofetil, or Azathioprine).
Phase 4: Biologics. Adalimumab (Humira) 40mg SC every 2 weeks or Infliximab (Remicade) for Behcet's or refractory cases.
Phase 5: Local Implants. Intravitreal Dexamethasone (Ozurdex) or Fluocinolone (Yutiq) for chronic non-infectious cases.

sections.title: Surgical Interventions
content: Diagnostic Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV) for masquerade/PCR.
Therapeutic PPV for clearing dense vitreous debris or vitreous hemorrhage.
Glaucoma surgery (Tube shunts preferred over trabeculectomy in active uveitis).
Cataract surgery: Must be 'quiet' for 3 months; use heavy perioperative steroid coverage.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Chronic CME: Leading cause of permanent central vision loss.
Cataract: Posterior Subcapsular (PSC) from both disease and steroids.
Epiretinal Membrane (ERM) and Macular Hole.
Band Keratopathy: Calcium deposits in the cornea.
Phthisis Bulbi: End-stage atrophy from ciliary body failure.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Recent Advances
content: SYPHILIS RULE: Always test for Syphilis; it is the 'Great Imitator' and can mimic any panuveitis pattern.
VISUAL I & II Trials: Established Adalimumab as the first non-steroid systemic therapy approved for non-infectious intermediate, posterior, and panuveitis.
Wide-field FFA: Essential to identify peripheral ischemia and vasculitis that standard photography misses.
STP Tapering: Never taper steroids faster than 5-10mg every 1-2 weeks once below 20mg/day to avoid rebound.
Biologics in Behcet's: Infliximab is often preferred for rapid control of sight-threatening Behcet's retinal vasculitis.
